primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease due to UMOD (ADTKD-UMOD)
mechanism: Pathogenic UMOD variants cause abnormal uromodulin folding and intracellular retention in the endoplasmic reticulum of thick ascending limb cells. This ER storage process produces chronic tubulointerstitial kidney disease, often with bland urine and early hyperuricemia/gout.
vignette: A 24-year-old man has slowly progressive chronic kidney disease, recurrent gout, and a bland urinalysis with minimal protein. His father and paternal grandfather developed kidney failure. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous pathogenic variant in UMOD.
lead: Which cellular abnormality most directly contributes to this patient's kidney disease?
correct: Intracellular retention of misfolded uromodulin in the endoplasmic reticulum of thick ascending limb cells
distractors: Defective endosomal chloride/proton exchange in proximal tubular cells
Failure of type IV collagen assembly in the glomerular basement membrane
Loss of polycystin-mediated signaling in primary cilia of tubular epithelial cells
Defective podocin localization at the slit diaphragm
distractor_notes: Proximal-tubule endosomal chloride/proton exchange is the CLCN5/ClC-5 mechanism of Dent disease, not UMOD-associated tubulointerstitial disease.
Type IV collagen defects cause Alport-spectrum glomerular basement membrane disease, which typically produces hematuria rather than bland tubulointerstitial CKD.
Polycystin dysfunction causes autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with cyst formation, not the UMOD ER-storage phenotype.
Podocin defects cause a glomerular filtration-barrier disorder with proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome, not bland tubulointerstitial disease.
key_expl: ADTKD-UMOD is an endoplasmic-reticulum storage disease. Pathogenic UMOD variants impair uromodulin folding, causing abnormal protein retention in thick ascending limb cells and progressive tubulointerstitial kidney disease.
objective: Link ADTKD-UMOD to endoplasmic-reticulum retention of abnormal uromodulin in thick ascending limb cells.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is a disorder of lysosome-related organelle biogenesis that causes oculocutaneous albinism and a platelet storage-pool defect with absent platelet delta (dense) granules; PT, PTT, and platelet count are typically normal.
vignette: An 8-year-old child with hypopigmented skin and hair, nystagmus, recurrent epistaxis, and easy bruising has a normal platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time. Whole-mount electron microscopy of platelets shows absent dense bodies.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this combination of findings?
distractors: Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Glanzmann thrombasthenia
von Willebrand disease
Isolated oculocutaneous albinism
distractor_notes: Chediak-Higashi syndrome features lysosomal trafficking defects with recurrent infections and giant cytoplasmic granules; absent platelet dense bodies plus the classic HPS phenotype is more specific here.
Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a GPIIb/IIIa platelet aggregation defect and does not cause oculocutaneous albinism.
von Willebrand disease can cause mucocutaneous bleeding but does not cause albinism or absent platelet delta granules.
Isolated oculocutaneous albinism does not explain the platelet dense-granule storage-pool defect and bleeding diathesis.
key_expl: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome combines oculocutaneous albinism with a bleeding diathesis caused by absent platelet delta granules; platelet count and routine coagulation times are typically normal.
objective: Recognize Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome from the combination of albinism, mucocutaneous bleeding, and absent platelet dense bodies.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
mechanism: HNPP is usually caused by a recurrent deletion involving PMP22 that reduces PMP22 dosage. PMP22 haploinsufficiency disrupts peripheral myelin and predisposes to recurrent focal neuropathies after compression or minor trauma.
vignette: A 27-year-old man has had several episodes of transient foot drop and hand numbness after prolonged leg crossing or leaning on his elbows. His father has a similar history. Nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy, and chromosomal microarray identifies a recurrent deletion at 17p11.2 involving PMP22.
lead: Which molecular consequence most directly causes this patient's disorder?
correct: PMP22 haploinsufficiency from reduced gene dosage
distractors: Increased PMP22 gene dosage from a reciprocal duplication
Gain-of-function mutation of a neuronal voltage-gated sodium channel
Loss of dystrophin-mediated linkage between actin and the extracellular matrix
Defective mitochondrial fusion caused by biallelic loss of MFN2
distractor_notes: A reciprocal PMP22-containing duplication at this locus is associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A rather than HNPP.
Neuronal sodium-channel gain-of-function causes channelopathies such as some epilepsy or pain syndromes, not the recurrent pressure palsy phenotype produced by PMP22 deletion.
Dystrophin deficiency causes Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy rather than a compression-sensitive demyelinating neuropathy.
MFN2 variants are associated with axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and are not the molecular consequence of the PMP22 deletion shown.
key_expl: HNPP is a PMP22 dosage disorder. The recurrent 17p11.2 deletion produces PMP22 haploinsufficiency, reducing peripheral myelin protein 22 and predisposing nerves to focal demyelination after pressure.
objective: Associate HNPP with reduced PMP22 gene dosage and haploinsufficiency.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
discipline: Bone Biology / Cell Biology / Medical Genetics
diagnosis: Hereditary multiple osteochondromas due to EXT1/EXT2 loss of function
mechanism: EXT1 and EXT2 encode transmembrane glycoproteins that form a heparan sulfate polymerase. Loss of EXT1/EXT2 function disrupts heparan sulfate biosynthesis and chondrocyte signaling, predisposing to multiple cartilage-capped osteochondromas arising from long-bone metaphyses.
vignette: A 12-year-old child has multiple painless, hard masses near the metaphyses of the distal femur and proximal tibia. Radiographs show multiple cartilage-capped osteochondromas. The child's father had similar lesions. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in EXT1.
lead: The affected gene product normally participates most directly in which process?
distractors: Hydroxylation of proline residues in procollagen
Gamma-carboxylation of osteocalcin
Hydrolysis of inorganic pyrophosphate by tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase
Proteolytic degradation of type I collagen by cathepsin K
distractor_notes: Prolyl hydroxylation is a collagen-processing step and is not the function of EXT1/EXT2.
Vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of osteocalcin is unrelated to EXT1/EXT2-associated osteochondroma formation.
TNSALP-mediated pyrophosphate hydrolysis is the ALPL pathway implicated in hypophosphatasia, not hereditary multiple osteochondromas.
Cathepsin K degrades bone matrix during osteoclastic resorption; EXT1/EXT2 instead form a heparan sulfate polymerase.
key_expl: EXT1 and EXT2 form a heterooligomeric heparan sulfate polymerase. Loss-of-function variants disrupt heparan sulfate-dependent signaling in growth-plate chondrocytes and cause hereditary multiple osteochondromas.
objective: Associate hereditary multiple osteochondromas with EXT1/EXT2-dependent heparan sulfate polymerization.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Danon disease is an X-linked LAMP2-related multisystem disorder in which males commonly develop severe childhood-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and conduction abnormalities together with skeletal myopathy and mild intellectual disability.
vignette: A 15-year-old boy is evaluated for exertional dyspnea and palpitations. Echocardiography shows marked concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, and ECG shows ventricular preexcitation. He also has mild proximal muscle weakness and longstanding learning difficulties. A maternal uncle died from cardiomyopathy in young adulthood.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this constellation of findings?
distractors: Pompe disease
Fabry disease
Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to a sarcomeric protein variant
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
distractor_notes: Pompe disease can cause cardiomyopathy and myopathy, especially in infancy, but the adolescent X-linked pattern with ventricular preexcitation, learning difficulties, and severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is more characteristic of Danon disease.

Fabry disease can cause left ventricular hypertrophy but typically has neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, renal involvement, and other alpha-galactosidase A manifestations rather than this classic Danon triad.
Isolated sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not explain the associated skeletal myopathy and cognitive phenotype.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy causes progressive proximal weakness and later dilated cardiomyopathy, not the characteristic severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/conduction phenotype described here.
key_expl: In affected males, Danon disease classically combines early severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and conduction abnormalities with skeletal muscle weakness and mild cognitive impairment; inheritance is X-linked through LAMP2.
objective: Recognize Danon disease from early hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/conduction disease plus skeletal myopathy and cognitive involvement in an X-linked pattern.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 (BSEP deficiency) due to ABCB11 dysfunction
mechanism: ABCB11 encodes the bile salt export pump (BSEP), an ATP-binding cassette transporter on the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes that mediates biliary bile-acid export. BSEP deficiency causes PFIC2 with cholestasis and typically low or normal GGT.
vignette: An infant develops progressive jaundice and intense pruritus. Laboratory studies show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with elevated aminotransferases but low gamma-glutamyl transferase activity. Genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in ABCB11.
lead: Which hepatocyte transport process is most directly impaired?
correct: ATP-dependent export of bile salts across the canalicular membrane into bile
distractors: Sodium-dependent uptake of bile salts across the basolateral membrane from portal blood
Canalicular secretion of conjugated bilirubin by MRP2
Canalicular export of phosphatidylcholine by MDR3
Basolateral export of bile acids from hepatocytes back into sinusoidal blood
distractor_notes: Basolateral sodium-dependent bile-salt uptake is mediated principally by NTCP, not ABCB11/BSEP.
MRP2 transports conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions; it is distinct from BSEP-mediated bile-salt export.
MDR3/ABCB4 exports phosphatidylcholine and is associated with PFIC3, which typically has elevated GGT.
Basolateral bile-acid efflux is a compensatory route in cholestasis but is not the normal canalicular BSEP function lost in PFIC2.
key_expl: ABCB11 encodes BSEP, the major canalicular bile-salt exporter. Loss of BSEP impairs ATP-dependent secretion of bile salts from hepatocytes into bile and produces PFIC2, often with low or normal GGT.
objective: Link ABCB11-related PFIC2 to impaired canalicular bile-salt export by BSEP.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Activating KCNJ11 variants reduce ATP inhibition of the Kir6.2-containing beta-cell KATP channel. The channel remains excessively open despite glucose metabolism, maintaining membrane hyperpolarization and suppressing voltage-gated calcium influx and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
vignette: A 10-week-old infant has persistent hyperglycemia and low endogenous insulin secretion without pancreatic agenesis. Genetic testing identifies an activating pathogenic variant in KCNJ11, which encodes the Kir6.2 subunit of the pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channel.
lead: Which beta-cell event is most directly prevented by this mutation after glucose enters the cell?
correct: ATP-dependent KATP-channel closure followed by membrane depolarization and calcium-triggered insulin release
distractors: Glucose uptake through GLUT2 at the beta-cell membrane
Conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate by glucokinase
Transcription of the insulin gene by PDX1
Proteolytic conversion of proinsulin to insulin and C-peptide
distractor_notes: KCNJ11 encodes the Kir6.2 KATP-channel subunit, not GLUT2; glucose entry can occur despite the channel defect.
Glucokinase is encoded by GCK and can generate the ATP signal; the activating KCNJ11 channel fails to close appropriately in response to that signal.
PDX1 regulates beta-cell gene transcription and pancreatic development but is not the immediate electrical coupling defect caused by activating KCNJ11 variants.
Proinsulin processing occurs downstream of insulin biosynthesis and does not explain the failure of glucose-stimulated electrical depolarization and secretion.
key_expl: Normally, glucose metabolism raises the ATP:ADP ratio, closing beta-cell KATP channels; this depolarizes the membrane, opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and triggers insulin release. Activating KCNJ11 variants reduce ATP-mediated channel closure, so the beta cell remains hyperpolarized and insulin secretion is suppressed.
objective: Explain KCNJ11-related neonatal diabetes through failure of ATP-sensitive potassium-channel closure and beta-cell depolarization.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: PMM2 encodes phosphomannomutase 2, which converts mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate. Loss of PMM2 lowers the mannose-1-phosphate/GDP-mannose pool and impairs synthesis of lipid-linked oligosaccharides required for N-linked protein glycosylation.
vignette: An infant has hypotonia, developmental delay, esotropia, inverted nipples, abnormal suprapubic fat pads, and cerebellar hypoplasia. Serum transferrin glycoform analysis suggests a congenital disorder of N-linked glycosylation, and genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in PMM2.
lead: Which metabolic conversion is most directly impaired?
distractors: Mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal hydrolases in the Golgi apparatus
Fructose-1-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde
Galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose
Glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone
distractor_notes: Failure to add mannose-6-phosphate tags to lysosomal enzymes is the GNPTAB-related mechanism of mucolipidosis II/III, not PMM2 deficiency.
Fructose-1-phosphate cleavage is catalyzed by aldolase B and is impaired in hereditary fructose intolerance.
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency causes classic galactosemia, not PMM2-CDG.
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase catalyzes the first oxidative step of the pentose phosphate pathway, unrelated to N-linked glycosylation.
key_expl: PMM2 is phosphomannomutase 2. It converts mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate, which feeds GDP-mannose and lipid-linked oligosaccharide synthesis for N-linked glycosylation.
objective: Link PMM2-CDG to impaired conversion of mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate and deficient N-linked glycosylation.
clues: inverted nipples and abnormal fat pads

mechanism: Immortal time bias arises when exposure is defined by a future event after cohort entry and pre-exposure follow-up is incorrectly attributed to the exposed group, creating a period during which exposed participants must, by definition, remain event-free long enough to receive the exposure.
vignette: Researchers use electronic records to compare mortality in patients with a new cancer diagnosis. Patients are classified as “treated” if they receive a particular drug at any time during the first 90 days after diagnosis, but follow-up for both groups begins on the date of diagnosis. Time from diagnosis until first drug dose is counted as treated person-time. A patient who dies before receiving the drug can only be classified as untreated.
lead: Which bias is introduced by this analysis?
distractors: Lead-time bias
Length-time bias
Confounding by indication
Recall bias
distractor_notes: Lead-time bias concerns apparent survival extension from earlier detection without changing the time of death; the problem here is exposure classification over follow-up.
Length-time bias arises because screening preferentially detects slower-growing disease; no screening-detection mechanism is described.

Confounding by indication can affect treatment studies, but the specific structural error described is assigning pre-exposure time to the treated group, during which participants had to survive to receive treatment.
Recall bias occurs when exposure or outcome information is remembered differently by groups; this electronic-record design instead has a time-classification problem.
key_expl: The treated group must survive from cohort entry until drug initiation, yet that pre-treatment interval is counted as treated follow-up. Because death cannot occur in that interval for someone who is ultimately classified as treated, the analysis contains immortal time bias.
objective: Recognize immortal time bias when pre-exposure follow-up is incorrectly classified as exposed person-time in an observational cohort.
clues: treated status requires surviving until drug initiation
early deaths forced into untreated group

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: A check-back is a closed-loop communication strategy in which the receiver repeats information back and the sender verifies or corrects the repeated message, reducing communication errors.
vignette: During an emergency department resuscitation, a laboratory technologist calls and reports a critical potassium result. The physician responds, “Potassium 2.6 mEq/L; I heard 2.6, correct?” The technologist confirms that the repeated value is correct.
lead: Which communication technique is being used?
distractors: SBAR handoff
Teach-back
Motivational interviewing
Shared decision-making
distractor_notes: SBAR structures a situation-background-assessment-recommendation handoff; the scenario instead verifies a specific transmitted message by repeating it back.
Teach-back asks a patient or caregiver to explain health information in their own words to confirm understanding; this is team closed-loop verification of a critical result.
Motivational interviewing explores ambivalence and elicits motivation for behavior change, which is not occurring here.
Shared decision-making integrates clinical evidence with patient values and preferences when choosing among options; the scenario is message verification.
key_expl: A check-back, also called repeat-back, is a closed-loop communication technique: the receiver repeats the information and the sender verifies that it was received accurately.
objective: Recognize check-back/repeat-back as a closed-loop technique for verifying critical information between team members.
